title: the smallest prayer
hookLine: forehead, chest, shoulder, shoulder: what the hand is tracing
carry: head, heart, shoulders — all of you

lines: A PITCHER. A GRANDMOTHER. A HOSPITAL HALLWAY.
cards: A pitcher does it before the first throw. A grandmother does it when the bus passes a church. Someone does it in a hospital hallway, right after the doctor leaves.
Forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other. Two seconds, no words out loud. If you grew up Catholic, your hand may know it better than your head does.
It's a prayer, maybe the smallest there is, and the hand is tracing something on purpose.

teach.h: A THUMB ON THE FOREHEAD, AROUND 200.

teach.b: Around the year 200, a Christian writer in North Africa described believers tracing a tiny cross on their foreheads all day long: getting dressed, sitting down to eat, lighting a lamp.
Over the centuries that thumb-sized cross grew into the big one. And it says two things at once. The hand traces the cross, the shape Jesus died on, over your own body.
The words name who Catholics believe God is.
They come from the end of Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus sends his friends out, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
One God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

teach.h: HOLY WATER: A REMINDER OF BAPTISM.
teach.b: That's why many Catholics dip their fingers in holy water at the church door first. Those same words were said over them, with water, at their baptism. Now look where the hand goes.
The forehead, where you think. The chest, where your heart is. The shoulders, where you carry things.
Many hear it that way: nothing left out. Western Catholics go to the left shoulder first; Orthodox Christians go right, then left. Same sign, two old habits.

how: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of the Mass, often after dipping their fingers in holy water on entering a church, touching forehead, chest, left shoulder and right shoulder.

games.q: what the hand is tracing — tap the pairs.

s: the sign of the cross started as a sports habit
Christians were tracing a small cross on their foreheads around the year 200.
the words come from the end of Matthew's Gospel
"in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost."
every Christian goes to the same shoulder first
Western Catholics usually go left, then right; Orthodox Christians go right, then left.

games.q: you walk into a Catholic church behind a family. in the custom this lesson describes, what do many of them do at the door?
o: dip their fingers in holy water and make the sign of the cross.
games.why: holy water, then the sign: a small reminder of the water and the words of their baptism.

games.q: put the sign back in order.

practice: One breath with the bell. If you'd like, make the sign slowly, slower than anyone ever does it: forehead, chest, left shoulder, right. Or just rest a hand on each place and notice it.
Then let the breath all the way out.

wordCard.voice: The sign of the cross. The cross traced over all of you, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. First word on your strand.

orig.s: In nomine Patris, et Filii, et Spiritus Sancti
orig.say: in NOH-mee-neh PAH-trees, et FEE-lee-ee, et SPEE-ree-toos SAHNK-tee
orig.note: Latin: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. the words said with the sign for centuries at the Latin Mass.

carryVoice: Your line: head, heart, shoulders — all of you. Two seconds, and nothing left out. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1668, 2157 (blessings and holy water; beginning the day with the sign of the cross)
